findings.title: Sort direction defaults to descending for every column when no prefix is given
findings.description: The query's `sort` convention is that a `-` prefix means descending, so an unprefixed value should mean ascending. The code computes `descending = sort.startswith('-')`, which is correct for that convention. The real problem is the default: `query.get('sort', '-placed')` keeps newest-first only when `sort` is absent. An explicit `sort=placed` therefore flips to ascending, which silently differs from the old default and from `orders_panel`'s own default of `descending=True`. Callers that pass `sort=total` or `sort=customer` get ascending results, while `orders_panel(sort='total')` gets descending. The two entry points disagree on the direction for the same column name.
findings.suggestion: Document and keep a single convention, or make the direction default consistent between `orders_panel` and `panel_from_query`.

findings.title: Blank status parameter is treated as no filter
findings.description: If `status` is empty, or contains only commas or whitespace (e.g. `status=,`), the parsed list is empty and `or None` turns it into None, so no status filter is applied. A user who explicitly sent an empty filter gets every order instead of a rejection or an empty result. `orders_between` has a deliberate branch for an empty `statuses` list, and it is unreachable from this entry point.
findings.suggestion: Pass None only when the `status` key is absent; otherwise pass the parsed list, or raise ValueError for a blank value.

findings.title: Sort prefix handling accepts a bare "-" and silently changes the sort direction
findings.description: `panel_from_query` derives the sort direction from a leading "-" and passes the remainder as the sort key. A bare "-" gives an empty key, which `orders_between` rejects with a confusing message ("cannot sort by ''"). A client sending `sort=placed` (no prefix) gets ascending order, while the default with no `sort` parameter is descending. This is documented, but easy to misuse.
findings.suggestion: Validate the stripped sort key and raise a clearer error for an empty one.

findings.title: Sort prefix handling breaks the "-" direction and the "+" convention
findings.description: `descending = sort.startswith("-")` treats any sort without a leading '-' as ascending. That is consistent with the documented API. However, in a URL query string a literal '+' prefix is decoded as a space, so `sort=+total` becomes ' total' and fails with a ValueError. Also, the default for orders_panel is descending=True but a plain `sort=total` from the query gives ascending, so behaviour differs between the two entry points. This is a minor contract inconsistency.
findings.suggestion: Strip whitespace and document that unprefixed means ascending, or keep the same default direction in both entry points.

findings.title: Empty status list is checked after unknown check but behaves differently from None
findings.description: An explicitly empty `statuses` list returns no orders, but `panel_from_query` converts an empty or blank status parameter to None, which returns all orders. Direct callers passing `[]` get an empty result while the query path gets everything; this inconsistency may surprise callers. It is arguably intentional.
findings.suggestion: Document the semantics clearly or treat empty as no filter in both places.

findings.title: DEFAULT_FLAGS silently merged in, changing is_enabled/require semantics
findings.description: snapshot() overlays the backend result on DEFAULT_FLAGS. Flags the backend omits now take DEFAULT_FLAGS values, so "invoice_pdf_export" and "search_suggestions" are on whenever the backend lacks them, including when the backend returns an empty dict for an environment. Before this change, unknown flags were off. require() guards unreleased endpoints, so any flag with a True default is now open by default, and a flag deleted in the backend turns on instead of off. Behaviour changes for all callers, not only those who opted into defaults.
findings.suggestion: Keep is_enabled/require fail-closed (use only backend values), or apply defaults only for explicitly opted-in flags and document the behaviour.

findings.title: Stale serving extends checked_at but the max_stale bound is checked against a possibly shifted 'now'
findings.description: On BackendUnavailable, `now` was captured before the backend call, which may have blocked for a long time (timeouts). The max_stale check at line 115 and checked_at use this pre-call timestamp, so a snapshot that has actually exceeded max_stale by the time the call failed can still be served and re-marked as checked. Staleness is understated by the backend call duration, and the stale window can overrun max_stale by up to ttl plus the call latency.
findings.suggestion: Re-read self._clock() after the failure and use that value for the max_stale comparison and for checked_at.

findings.title: Shared global `evolve` function is mutated by `_add_method_dunders`
findings.description: `_add_method_dunders` sets `__module__`, `__qualname__` and `__doc__` on the object it receives. The old code passed a fresh wrapper per class. Now it passes the module-level `attr.evolve` itself. Each decorated class overwrites `evolve.__module__`, `evolve.__qualname__` and `evolve.__doc__` globally. After that, `attr.evolve` reports a wrong qualname and module (for example `SomeClass.evolve`), and its docs and repr are corrupted. The same function object is also shared across all classes, so the last class to be processed wins.
findings.suggestion: Keep a per-class wrapper so the dunder fix-ups apply to it rather than to `evolve`: `def __replace__(self, /, **changes): return evolve(self, **changes)`, then pass that to `_add_method_dunders`.

findings.title: Shared `evolve` function is mutated by `_add_method_dunders`
findings.description: `_add_method_dunders` sets `__module__`, `__qualname__` and `__doc__` on the function it receives. The old code passed a fresh wrapper per class, so this was harmless. Now it receives the global `attr.evolve` object, so every class that uses `__replace__` rewrites the public `evolve` function's metadata. After that, `evolve.__module__`, `evolve.__qualname__` and `evolve.__doc__` point at whichever class was built last. This breaks introspection, docs and repr of `evolve`, and the same function object is shared across all classes.
findings.suggestion: Keep a per-class wrapper so the dunders are set on the wrapper, not on `evolve`: `def __replace__(self, /, **changes): return evolve(self, **changes)`.

findings.title: Shared `evolve` function is mutated by `_add_method_dunders`
findings.description: `_add_method_dunders` assigns `__module__`, `__qualname__` and `__doc__` on the function it receives. The old code passed a fresh per-class wrapper. Now it passes the global `attr.evolve` function itself, so every class built with `add_replace` overwrites the metadata of the shared function. `attr.evolve` then reports the last decorated class's module, qualname and a generated docstring. The same function object is also used as `__replace__` on every class, so all of them share one metadata set. This breaks introspection, docs and pickling by qualified name.
findings.suggestion: Keep a per-class wrapper so the dunder assignment touches a fresh function, for example `def __replace__(*args, **changes): return evolve(*args, **changes)`. Alternatively, skip `_add_method_dunders` and assign `evolve` directly.

findings.title: Stale heap entries are no longer skipped, so expiry can use the wrong timestamp
findings.description: The removed `_is_current` check detected heap entries that were superseded when an item was re-added. Now `self._heap[0][0]` is used directly, even if that entry is stale. A stale head with an old timestamp makes the loop call `pop()` on a re-added, still-fresh item (and `pop()` then discards the stale entry and removes the live item). A stale head with a newer timestamp can instead stop the loop early. Either way, expiry is wrong and live items can be evicted prematurely.
findings.suggestion: Keep the `_is_current` check (compare the heap entry with `self._data.get(item)`), and discard stale heap entries before comparing timestamps.

findings.title: pop() removes a live item when it pops a stale heap entry
findings.description: `pop()` now removes `item` from `_data` whenever the key exists, without checking that the popped heap entry is the current one. If an item was re-added, its old entry is still in the heap. Popping that old entry deletes the newer live item from `_data` and returns it as the oldest item. The newer heap entry then becomes stale. This breaks the ordering guarantee, and items can be evicted early.
findings.suggestion: Verify that `self._data.get(item) is entry` before deleting. Otherwise skip the stale entry.

findings.title: Stale heap entries are treated as current, so re-added items are evicted early
findings.description: The removed `_is_current` check compared the heap entry with the one stored in `_data`. It is replaced with a check on key presence alone. If an item is discarded or re-added (for example via `add` after `discard`/`update`), the old heap entry stays in the heap. `pop()` now accepts that stale entry whenever the key exists in `_data`, so it evicts the newly re-added item based on the old timestamp and position. Expiry and size-limit eviction therefore remove items too early and in the wrong order.
findings.suggestion: Restore the identity check, `self._data.get(item) is entry`, before deleting from `_data`, and skip stale entries.

findings.title: Expiry check uses the timestamp of a possibly stale heap head
findings.description: Stale entries are no longer skipped before `self._heap[0][0]` is read. A stale head with an old timestamp can trigger `pop()` for a fresher live item. Conversely, a stale head with a recent timestamp can break the loop while genuinely expired items remain behind it. Either way the expiry decision is wrong.
findings.suggestion: Pop stale heap heads before reading the timestamp, as the removed code did.

findings.title: Stale heap entries for re-added items evict the live entry early
findings.description: The pop path no longer checks that the heap entry is the current one for the item. When an item is re-added, the old heap entry stays in the heap and the newer one is in `_data`. Popping the stale entry removes the live item, so the item is evicted early using the old insertion time, and its newer heap entry becomes stale. The expiry loop at line 633 also reads `self._heap[0][0]` without validating it, so a stale entry's timestamp can wrongly decide that the live item has expired or not.
findings.suggestion: Restore the `_is_current(entry)` check in `pop()` and in the expiry loop, and discard stale entries from the heap head before using their timestamps.

findings.title: del of _message_formatter raises AttributeError when no instance attribute is set
findings.description: `del conn._message_formatter` removes an instance attribute. If the attribute was never set on the instance (for example `logging_token=None` passed on a connection that never had a token, or a second reset), this raises AttributeError. If it is a class-level default, instance deletion fails the same way. The previous code assigned None, which was always safe. Clearing the token via execution_options can therefore crash.
findings.suggestion: Restore `conn._message_formatter = None`, or guard the delete with `conn.__dict__.pop('_message_formatter', None)`.

findings.title: del of _message_formatter can raise AttributeError when no instance attribute is set
findings.description: The `else` branch now runs `del conn._message_formatter`. If `logging_token` is set to a falsy value (None or empty string) when no formatter was previously set on this Connection instance, the instance has no such attribute to delete and `del` raises AttributeError. The old code assigned None, which never failed. This happens for `execution_options(logging_token=None)` on a fresh connection, and for a repeated falsy call. It may also fail if `_message_formatter` is a class-level attribute or a slot, or if other code expects the attribute to exist.
findings.suggestion: Restore the safe assignment (`conn._message_formatter = None`), or guard the delete with `conn.__dict__.pop('_message_formatter', None)`.

findings.title: del on _message_formatter can raise AttributeError when no instance attribute is set
findings.description: The `else` branch now does `del conn._message_formatter`. If the attribute was never assigned on the instance (e.g. `logging_token` is set to None or empty on a connection that never had a token), the `del` raises AttributeError. It will also fail if the attribute is a class-level default or slot that was never assigned. The previous code assigned None, which always worked. A call such as `execution_options(logging_token=None)` can now crash.
findings.suggestion: Restore the safe assignment (`conn._message_formatter = None`), or guard the deletion with `if hasattr(...)` or `conn.__dict__.pop('_message_formatter', None)`.

findings.title: Falsy data_key (empty string) now falls back to field_name
findings.description: The original code only fell back to field_name when data_key was None. Using `or` also treats an empty string as missing. A field declared with data_key="" is a valid explicit key, since the Field code only checks `is not None`. With this change, Pluck would serialize and deserialize under field_name instead of "", while the inner schema uses "". The two sides then disagree, which breaks the round trip and the error keys.
findings.suggestion: Restore the explicit None check: `return only_field.data_key if only_field.data_key is not None else self.field_name`.

findings.title: Falsy data_key (empty string) now falls back to field_name
findings.description: The change replaces an explicit `is not None` check with `or`. A field declared with `data_key=""` is valid and gets the empty string as its key everywhere else in the schema. This property now returns `field_name` instead. The `Pluck` field then reads and writes the wrong key when serializing and deserializing a plucked field whose data_key is an empty string. This is an edge case.
findings.suggestion: Restore the explicit check: `return only_field.data_key if only_field.data_key is not None else self.field_name`.

findings.title: Truthiness check replaces explicit None check for data_key
findings.description: `only_field.data_key or self.field_name` treats an empty-string data_key as unset, whereas the previous code only fell back when data_key was None. A field declared with data_key="" now resolves to the field name instead of the empty key. The key used for serialization and deserialization elsewhere in marshmallow still honors the empty string, so the Pluck key can disagree with the schema's own key. This is an edge case.
findings.suggestion: Restore the explicit check: `return only_field.data_key if only_field.data_key is not None else self.field_name`.

findings.title: Rounded-up start can fall outside window or be pushed past the slot's free end, and tz-aware math is fragile
findings.description: `_round_up` is applied to `free.start`, but `common_free_time` only guarantees a free interval of at least `length`. After rounding, the while-condition handles the end correctly, so the rounded slot is skipped if it no longer fits. However, when `step` does not divide an hour (e.g. 45 or 7 minutes), `(moment - hour) % step` gives phases that drift hour to hour. The docstring promises multiples of step past the hour, but later slots generated by `start += step` cross hour boundaries and stop being aligned. Slots are therefore misaligned, and a step greater than an hour gives odd results.
findings.suggestion: Require `step` to divide 60 minutes in `__post_init__`, or align each candidate start by recomputing from its own hour.

findings.title: Overlap check only against last pick; non-overlap contract and step spacing interplay
findings.description: `suggest` skips slots that overlap the last pick, which with a small step (default 1 minute) means the picks are back-to-back slots, ignoring `buffer` between suggestions. Also, `first_slot` previously returned the free interval's start exactly. It now returns the start rounded up, which changes results by up to a step (the default 1 minute only affects non-whole-minute starts, e.g. 09:00:30 becomes 09:01). This is a behavior change for existing callers.
findings.suggestion: Keep exact start when the step is the default, or round only when the start is not already aligned to a whole-minute boundary. Document the change.

findings.title: Rounding free-interval start can push slot start outside the window or free interval
findings.description: _round_up is applied to free.start. When rounding moves start past free.end - length, the while loop yields nothing, so a free interval that previously produced a valid slot at free.start is now skipped. first_slot previously returned Interval(free.start, ...) and now may raise NoCommonSlot, or skip to a later slot, whenever the free gap is only slightly longer than length and free.start is not aligned to step. Default step is 1 minute, but sub-minute seconds or microseconds in the start also trigger rounding.
findings.suggestion: This is intended behavior if alignment is required, but document it. Otherwise fall back to free.start when the rounded start does not fit, or choose the default step so existing callers are unaffected.

findings.title: Overlap check only compares to last pick, and with step < length makes suggestions dense
findings.description: Candidate slots are generated `step` apart (default 1 minute), so consecutive candidates overlap heavily. The loop skips candidates until one doesn't overlap the last pick, which works. However, the check is only against picks[-1], and the slots from different free intervals never overlap. The real issue: picks are adjacent back-to-back with no buffer between suggestions, so suggestions are immediately consecutive. Minor.
findings.suggestion: Optionally require a gap between picks, or spread suggestions across free intervals.

findings.title: _round_up modulo uses hour-relative offset, wrong for steps not dividing an hour
findings.description: The remainder is computed relative to the top of the hour, so for a step that does not divide 60 minutes (e.g. 25 or 45 minutes, or >1 hour), alignment resets every hour and is not a consistent multiple. Steps longer than an hour yield remainder = whole offset and round up to the wrong time (moment + step - remainder), not necessarily a multiple of anything meaningful. Subsequent `start += step` also drifts from the hour grid.
findings.suggestion: Validate that step divides one hour evenly, or round relative to a fixed epoch or the window start.

findings.title: Generator `rows` is consumed by the rejected-list pass, so no rows are imported
findings.description: `parse_rows` now returns a generator. Line 35 iterates it to the end to build `rejected`. The loop at line 39 then iterates an exhausted generator, so `book.upsert` is never called. Every import silently returns created=0 and updated=0, with only the rejected list filled in. The previous list return value made two passes safe.
findings.suggestion: Materialise the rows before the two passes with `rows = list(parse_rows(lines))`. To keep streaming, collect the valid rows in a single pass and only upsert them after the error-count check.

findings.title: parse_rows is now a one-shot generator but is iterated twice
findings.description: parse_rows now returns a generator. The list comprehension on line 35 consumes it fully to collect rejected rows, so the `for row in rows` loop on line 39 iterates an exhausted generator. No valid row is ever upserted, and the report comes back with created=0 and updated=0 while appearing to succeed. Previously parse_rows returned a list, so iterating twice worked.
findings.suggestion: Materialise the rows with `rows = list(parse_rows(lines))`. That also keeps the guarantee that nothing is written before the error threshold is checked. Alternatively, upsert valid rows in a single pass, but that would break the 'nothing written' guarantee.

findings.title: Header validation error is now raised lazily
findings.description: Because parse_rows is now a generator, the ValueError for missing columns is raised on first iteration, not when parse_rows is called. Any caller that wrapped the call itself in try/except to catch the error will no longer catch it. Within import_csv it still happens before any write, so only direct callers are affected.
findings.suggestion: Validate the header eagerly in a non-generator wrapper function and return the inner generator from it, or document that the error surfaces on iteration.

findings.title: Generator `rows` is consumed by the rejected-list comprehension, so no valid rows are imported
findings.description: parse_rows now returns a generator. Line 35 iterates it fully to build `rejected`, so the later `for row in rows` loop at line 39 sees an exhausted iterator and imports nothing. Every import reports created=0 and updated=0 while silently dropping all valid contacts. The previous list return value made the double iteration safe.
findings.suggestion: Materialise the rows with `rows = list(parse_rows(lines))`. This also keeps the check-before-write guarantee. For true streaming of large files, validate in a first pass over a re-openable source and write in a second pass.

findings.title: Missing-columns ValueError now raised lazily at first iteration
findings.description: parse_rows is now a generator function, so the header validation no longer runs when it is called. It runs on the first `next()`. The ValueError for missing columns still propagates out of import_csv in practice, but any caller that calls parse_rows outside a try block and iterates later will see the error at an unexpected place. Callers also cannot rely on validation having happened once parse_rows returns.
findings.suggestion: Split into an eager function that validates the header and returns an inner generator, or document and handle the lazy behaviour.

findings.title: ZoneConfig.duration changed from seconds to milliseconds
findings.description: Previously `duration` was `minutes * 60`, i.e. seconds. It is now set to `run_time`, which `parse_duration` returns in milliseconds. Consumers such as the scheduler (`Run.seconds`) and the controller's `self._sleep(run.seconds)` treat the value as seconds. Every zone will therefore water for 1000 times its configured time (a 10 minute zone would run for about 167 hours), for both the old `minutes` and the new `duration` formats.
findings.suggestion: Convert to seconds when building the zone, e.g. `duration=run_time / 1000`, or change the field and all its consumers to milliseconds.

findings.title: ZoneConfig.duration changes unit from seconds to milliseconds
findings.description: `duration` used to be `minutes * 60`, i.e. seconds. It is now `run_time`, the millisecond value returned by `parse_duration`. The controller sleeps for `run.seconds`, which is presumably derived from `zone.duration`. Every zone, including those using the legacy `minutes` key, would then water for 1000x its configured time (a 10-minute zone runs about 167 hours). That risks flooding and wasted water.
findings.suggestion: Convert to seconds when building the zone, e.g. `duration=run_time / 1000`. Alternatively, store `duration_ms` and convert at the consumer.

findings.title: ZoneConfig.duration changes unit from seconds to milliseconds
findings.description: Previously `duration=minutes * 60` held seconds. It now holds `run_time` from parse_duration, which is in milliseconds. Nothing in the diff converts it back. The scheduler's `Run.seconds` presumably derives from `zone.duration` (not shown), and the controller passes `run.seconds` to `sleep`. Every zone would then water 1000 times longer than configured: a 10-minute zone would run for about 167 hours.
findings.suggestion: Store seconds: `duration=run_time / 1000`. Alternatively rename the field to `duration_ms` and update every consumer.

findings.title: OSError during write is swallowed; put() reports success without storing the blob
findings.description: If open, write, fsync or os.replace raises OSError (disk full, permission denied, I/O error), the handler removes the temp file and falls through to return BlobInfo(key, len(data)). The caller is told the blob was stored, but nothing exists on disk, so later get() calls raise BlobNotFound and the data is lost. The previous code propagated the error.
findings.suggestion: Re-raise after cleanup: `except OSError: tmp.unlink(missing_ok=True); raise`, or use `except BaseException`.

findings.title: OSError during write is swallowed, put() reports success without storing
findings.description: If open, write, fsync or os.replace fails (disk full, permission denied, I/O error), the except block removes the temp file and then falls through to `return BlobInfo(key, len(data))`. The caller is told the blob was stored, but nothing exists on disk, so a later get() raises BlobNotFound. This is silent data loss. The previous code propagated the error.
findings.suggestion: Re-raise after cleanup: `except OSError: tmp.unlink(missing_ok=True); raise`, or use `except BaseException`/finally for cleanup.

findings.title: OSError during write is swallowed and put() reports success
findings.description: If open, write, fsync or replace raises OSError (disk full, permission denied, I/O error), the handler removes the temp file and then falls through to `return BlobInfo(key, len(data))`. The caller is told the blob was stored, but nothing exists on disk, so a later get() raises BlobNotFound. This is silent data loss. The previous code propagated the error.
findings.suggestion: Re-raise after cleanup: `except OSError: tmp.unlink(missing_ok=True); raise`. Better, use `except BaseException` for the cleanup and re-raise.

findings.title: reserve_order is not atomic: partial reservations remain on failure
findings.description: reserve_order reserves lines one by one. If a later line raises UnknownSku or OutOfStock, the earlier lines stay reserved, and place_order returns 404/409 without rolling them back. The old code checked every line before reserving any, so a rejected order left no stock held. Now a rejected multi-line order permanently leaks reserved stock, making it unavailable to other orders.
findings.suggestion: Validate all lines first (existence and availability) before mutating anything, or track the reservations made so far and call release() for each in an except block before re-raising.

findings.title: reserve_order is not atomic: partial reservations leak on failure
findings.description: reserve_order reserves lines one at a time. If a later line raises OutOfStock or UnknownSku, earlier lines stay reserved. place_order then returns 409/404, but the stock held for the first lines is never released. Repeated failed orders permanently reduce available stock. The old code checked every line before reserving any, so this change introduces the regression.
findings.suggestion: Validate all lines first (existence and availability) before mutating anything, or roll back with release() for the lines already reserved when an exception occurs.

findings.title: reserve_order is not atomic: partial reservations leak on failure
findings.description: reserve_order reserves lines one at a time. If a later line raises UnknownSku or OutOfStock, the earlier lines stay reserved. place_order then returns 404 or 409, so the client sees a failed order while stock for the earlier lines is held and never released. The old code checked every line before reserving any, so this change introduces the leak.
findings.suggestion: Validate all lines first (check each SKU exists and has enough available stock), then apply the reservations. Alternatively, roll back the reservations already made when an exception occurs, using release.

findings.title: Window start can be negative when the body is shorter than width
findings.description: When a match is found and len(tokens) < width, len(tokens) - width is negative, so min() returns a negative start. The slice tokens[start:end] then uses negative indexing and returns the wrong words, usually an empty or truncated snippet. Also start > 0 is False, and end < len(tokens) can be True, so the truncation flags are wrong. Likewise, a hit near the start gives hit - width//2 < 0, so the window is anchored on a negative index instead of 0.
findings.suggestion: Clamp the start: start = max(0, min(hit - width // 2, len(tokens) - width)).

findings.title: Window start can be negative, producing wrong slice
findings.description: start = min(hit - width // 2, len(tokens) - width) is not clamped at 0. If the match is near the beginning (hit < width // 2), the first term is negative, so start is negative. If the body has fewer than `width` tokens, len(tokens) - width is negative too. tokens[start:end] with a negative start counts from the end of the list, so the slice is wrong (often empty or a few trailing words). For example, with 30 tokens, width 24 and hit 3, start = -9 and end = 15, so tokens[-9:15] is empty. Also start > 0 is false, so the snippet looks like an empty, untruncated string.
findings.suggestion: Clamp the start at 0: start = max(0, min(hit - width // 2, len(tokens) - width)).

findings.title: Start index can be negative when a match is near the beginning
findings.description: start = min(hit - width // 2, len(tokens) - width) is never clamped at 0. If the match is within the first width//2 words (e.g. hit=3, width=24), hit - 12 is negative, so start is negative. tokens[start:end] then uses negative slice indices: with start=-9 and end=15 the slice is tokens[-9:15], which is empty or wrong for longer bodies. The snippet is empty or wrong, and start > 0 is False, so no leading ellipsis is shown. The same happens for bodies shorter than width, where len(tokens) - width is negative.
findings.suggestion: Clamp the start at zero: start = max(0, min(hit - width // 2, len(tokens) - width)).

findings.title: Inbound count includes already-received purchase orders
findings.description: inbound_by_sku counts every order that is not CANCELLED. `OrderBook.orders` holds every PO ever raised, so orders that have already been received are counted as inbound too. Those units are already in `on_hand`, so they get counted twice. The position is overstated, and SKUs that need stock can be skipped or under-ordered. The effect grows as order history accumulates. This contradicts the docstring, which says inbound means units not in stock yet.
findings.suggestion: Count only open statuses, for example `if order.status in (POStatus.DRAFT, POStatus.SENT)`. Check the real POStatus members in stock/models.py.

findings.title: Received purchase orders are counted as inbound stock
findings.description: inbound_by_sku only skips CANCELLED orders. OrderBook keeps every PO ever raised, so orders already received (and so already counted in on_hand) are counted again as inbound. The inventory position is inflated by the full historical order quantity. SKUs then stop being reordered, or are under-ordered, which defeats the nightly job. This contradicts the docstring, which says inbound means units "not in stock yet".
findings.suggestion: Count only open statuses, for example DRAFT and SENT or whatever the model defines as outstanding. Exclude RECEIVED as well as CANCELLED, and subtract any partially received quantity.

findings.title: Inbound count includes already-received purchase orders
findings.description: inbound_by_sku only skips CANCELLED orders. The OrderBook holds every PO ever raised, so received/closed orders are also counted as inbound. Their units are already in on_hand, so they are counted twice. Over time the available position is inflated, SKUs stop hitting the reorder point, and reorder quantities shrink or drop to zero, leading to stock-outs.
findings.suggestion: Count only orders that are still outstanding (for example DRAFT/SENT/CONFIRMED), and exclude RECEIVED as well as CANCELLED. An explicit allow-list of open statuses is safer than a deny-list.

findings.title: Plan is switched before computing proration, so the credit uses the new plan's price
findings.description: change_plan assigns self.plan = new_plan on line 71 and only then calls plan_change_lines(self, new_plan, on). That function reads old_plan = sub.plan, which is now the new plan. The 'Unused <old>' credit is therefore priced and named from the new plan, so the credit and charge use the same price and the adjustment is wrong for every plan change. The history is also mutated before the call, so if split_period raises ValueError (e.g. `on` outside the period) the subscription is left on the new plan with a history entry and no adjustment.
findings.suggestion: Compute adjustment = plan_change_lines(self, new_plan, on) first, while self.plan is still the old plan, then set self.plan, append to history and extend pending_lines.

findings.title: Plan is swapped before proration is computed, so credit uses the new plan's price
findings.description: change_plan assigns self.plan = new_plan on line 71 and only then calls plan_change_lines(self, new_plan, on). Inside, old_plan = sub.plan is already the new plan. The credit line is therefore computed from the new plan's price and named after the new plan, so the 'Unused' credit and the new-plan charge are both for the new plan. Customers get wrong amounts and a wrong description on every plan change. In addition, if plan_change_lines raises ValueError because `on` is outside the period, the plan and history have already been mutated, leaving partial state.
findings.suggestion: Compute the adjustment before mutating: call plan_change_lines(self, new_plan, on) while self.plan is still the old plan, then set self.plan and append to history.

findings.title: Plan is switched before the proration is computed, so the credit uses the new plan's price
findings.description: change_plan sets self.plan = new_plan on line 71 and only then calls plan_change_lines(self, new_plan, on). Inside that function, old_plan = sub.plan is already new_plan. The 'Unused <old>' credit is therefore computed from the new plan's price and carries the new plan's name. The net adjustment is always roughly zero, and customers are under- or over-charged on every upgrade or downgrade. The history entry is also appended before validation, so if plan_change_lines raises (e.g. `on` outside the period), the subscription is left on the new plan with a history record but no adjustment lines.
findings.suggestion: Compute `adjustment = plan_change_lines(self, new_plan, on)` first, while self.plan is still the old plan. Then set self.plan, append to history, and extend pending_lines.

findings.title: build_invoice drains pending lines as a side effect
findings.description: build_invoice calls sub.take_pending_lines(), which clears the queue. Any repeated call for the same period (a preview, a retry, or re-rendering after a failure) silently loses the proration lines. The queued adjustments are also removed before the Invoice is persisted, so if a later step fails they are gone for good.
findings.suggestion: Read the pending lines without clearing them when building the invoice, and clear them only after the invoice has been committed or issued.

findings.title: Off-by-one: `until` day is excluded from the report
findings.description: The docstring says the range is inclusive, and the filter on line 38 keeps sales dated `until`. But `days = (until - since).days` combined with `range(days)` generates only `since` through `until - 1`. The last day is never emitted, so its sales are dropped from the rows and the totals. If since == until, the report is empty.
findings.suggestion: Use `range(days + 1)`, i.e. `days = (until - since).days + 1`.

findings.title: Empty export with both --since and --until falls through to the report
findings.description: When the export has no sales and both flags are given, the code continues to build the zero-filled report rather than printing 'no sales in export'. The condition is only partly consistent: with one flag missing it prints the message, with both it prints zero rows. This is arguably intended, but the behaviour differs depending on the flags.
findings.suggestion: Decide on one behaviour for an empty export and apply it regardless of the flags.

findings.title: Off-by-one: `until` day is excluded from the report
findings.description: The docstring promises rows from `since` to `until` inclusive, but `days = (until - since).days` and `range(days)` generate only `days` rows, covering `since` through `until - 1`. The last day is always dropped, even though sales on it were counted. When since == until, the result is an empty list. The report and its totals therefore omit the final day's sales.
findings.suggestion: Use `range(days + 1)`, e.g. `days = (until - since).days + 1`.

findings.title: Empty export with both --since and --until falls through, and `or` is used for optional dates
findings.description: When the export is empty but both dates are given, the code proceeds to a zero-row report, while a missing bound prints "no sales in export". That inconsistency is intentional enough, but the guard is also hit when sales exist but all are filtered out by --store, which is not handled. In that case, if --since/--until are omitted, the min/max is taken over unfiltered sales, so the range reflects other stores' days and not the selected store's. The result is zero rows for days the selected store never traded.
findings.suggestion: Compute default bounds from the store-filtered sales, or document that the bounds come from the whole export.

findings.title: Off-by-one: `until` day is excluded from the report
findings.description: The docstring says the range is inclusive, and sales on `until` pass the filter. But `days = (until - since).days` is used with `range(days)`, which yields only `days` rows, so the last day is never emitted. Calling with since == until returns an empty list. With the default `until` (the last sale day), the final day's sales are dropped from the rows and from the total.
findings.suggestion: Use `range(days + 1)`, i.e. `days = (until - since).days + 1`.

findings.title: Empty export with both --since and --until falls through, or the empty check is inconsistent
findings.description: When there are no sales and both bounds are given, it prints a zero-filled report, but with one bound missing it prints 'no sales in export'. Also, `args.since or ...` uses truthiness, which is fine for dates, but a missing bound combined with an empty store filter is not handled. If all sales are filtered out by --store, min/max still use the unfiltered sales, so the range spans all stores. This is only a minor inconsistency.
findings.suggestion: Treat the empty-export case uniformly, and compute default bounds from the store-filtered sales.

findings.title: store.project() called once per entry (N+1 lookups)
findings.description: Inside the loop over all entries, store.project(entry.project_id) is called for every entry, even though the same project repeats many times. If the store hits the database, this causes one query per timesheet entry, which is slow for large periods.
findings.suggestion: Only fetch a project when its id is not already in the `projects` dict, or fetch all projects in one batch call after the loop.

findings.title: Per-entry store.project() lookup (N+1)
findings.description: store.project() is called for every timesheet entry, even though only a few distinct projects exist. If the store hits a database or file, this is one query per entry for a period with thousands of entries, which slows the report badly.
findings.suggestion: Only look up a project when its id is not already in `projects`, or fetch all needed projects in one batch call after the loop, as is done for employees.

findings.title: store.project() called once per entry (N+1 lookups)
findings.description: Inside the entries loop, store.project(entry.project_id) is invoked for every entry, although the same project repeats many times. If the store hits the database, this causes one query per entry on a large period.
findings.suggestion: Only fetch the project when entry.project_id is not already in the projects dict, or batch-load projects after the loop like employees.

findings.title: Index re-parsed for every object during garbage collection
findings.description: `self._live_entries()` reads and JSON-parses the whole index file on every loop iteration, and then scans every entry linearly. With N objects and M index records this is O(N*M) work plus N full file reads, which gets very slow on large stores.
findings.suggestion: Compute the set of live digests once before the loop: `live = {e.digest for e in self._live_entries().values()}`, then test `path.name in live`.

findings.title: Index re-parsed for every object during garbage collection
findings.description: `self._live_entries()` reads and JSON-parses the whole index file on every loop iteration, and then scans all entries linearly. For N objects and M index records this costs O(N*M) parsing work, so GC on a large store becomes very slow.
findings.suggestion: Compute the set of live digests once before the loop, e.g. `live = {e.digest for e in self._live_entries().values()}`, and test `path.name in live`.

findings.title: Index re-read and re-parsed for every object during GC
findings.description: `_live_entries()` replays the whole index file inside the loop for each object file, and then the result is scanned linearly with `any`. Cost is O(objects × index records), so GC becomes very slow on stores with many blobs or a long append-only index.
findings.suggestion: Compute `live_digests = {e.digest for e in self._live_entries().values()}` once before the loop and test `path.name in live_digests`.

findings.title: Fetching page N re-walks all N-1 earlier pages (quadratic requests)
findings.description: episode_page reaches page `number` by fetching every earlier page just to collect its next_cursor. Each resumed import step therefore costs `number+1` requests. A full import of P pages makes about P²/2 requests. This multiplies rate-limit pressure, and a RateLimited error is more likely partway through the walk. A resumed import also repeats all the earlier pages before it makes progress.
findings.suggestion: Persist the next cursor with the checkpoint and resume from it, falling back to a re-walk only when the cursor has expired. Alternatively, have the import loop carry the cursor between pages instead of addressing pages by number.

findings.title: Page past the end is returned as an empty page, indistinguishable from a real empty last page
findings.description: If the cursor chain ends before reaching `number`, the method returns an empty EpisodePage with has_more=False. If the catalogue shrank, or the checkpoint is stale, the importer treats this as a normal completion and calls mark_imported. The import is then permanently marked complete, even though episodes may have been missed.
findings.suggestion: Make this case explicit, for example by raising an error or flagging it, and have the importer reset or verify the checkpoint instead of marking the import complete.

findings.title: mark_imported insert on a missing row leaves next_page at 0 and ignores checkpoint state
findings.description: mark_imported inserts a row with only completed_at when none exists. In that case next_page defaults to 0. This is inconsistent with the checkpoint. If reset_import is later used to clear completed_at, the whole state row is deleted, and a restart begins from page 0 with no record of earlier progress. This is mostly harmless because upserts are idempotent.

findings.title: Fetching page N re-walks all N-1 earlier pages (quadratic requests)
findings.description: episode_page(number) issues `number` requests just to walk cursors, then one more for the page itself. import_back_catalogue calls it for every page, so importing P pages costs about P²/2 requests. A resumed import also replays every earlier page before doing any new work. This makes rate limiting (RateLimited) far more likely on large back catalogues. Any 429 raised during the walk discards progress for that call.
findings.suggestion: Keep the cursor between calls within one import run and fall back to page-number walking only when resuming. Alternatively, persist a cursor and refresh it when it expires.

findings.title: mark_imported inserts a row with next_page defaulting to 0 when none exists
findings.description: This is only a problem when no row exists yet, so it is an edge path. In that case the upsert inserts next_page=0, and a later reset or checkpoint reads back 0. Normal flow saves a checkpoint first, so the path is mostly latent. The larger concern is that completion is stored separately from the checkpoint, so a crash between save_checkpoint and mark_imported is recoverable but not atomic.
findings.suggestion: Do the final page save and mark_imported in one transaction.

findings.title: Page upserts and checkpoint are not atomic; other ApiErrors leave progress inconsistent
findings.description: Episodes are upserted one at a time in separate transactions, followed by a separate checkpoint save. A crash mid-page re-imports that page on resume, which is idempotent but inflates the updated count. Only RateLimited is caught. Any other ApiError from episode_page propagates out of import_shows and aborts the whole run for all remaining shows, losing the ImportRun results.
findings.suggestion: Catch ApiError per show and record it in the result so the remaining shows continue.

findings.title: episode_page walks all prior pages from the start on every call
findings.description: To reach page N, the loop requests pages 0..N-1 one by one just to follow cursors, then fetches page N. Importing a show with P pages therefore costs about P^2/2 API calls. Resuming from a checkpoint repeats the whole walk. This makes rate limiting (429) far more likely, and a RateLimited raised during the walk discards all progress for that call.
findings.suggestion: Make the importer carry the cursor forward between pages, so each page costs one request. If a cursor must be persisted, store it with its issue time and fall back to the page-number walk only when it has expired.

findings.title: mark_imported on a fresh row leaves next_page at 0 and reset_import loses data
findings.description: mark_imported shares a row with the checkpoint. When the show is marked imported, the state is only valid if next_page was saved. Also, reset_import deletes both the checkpoint and the completion marker. That is probably intended, but any later re-import then restarts from page 0, and nothing here tells callers the checkpoint is gone. This is low-risk, but the coupling is fragile.
findings.suggestion: Keep checkpoint and completion consistent, for example by setting both in one statement.

findings.title: Checkpoint saved before completion is recorded; non-atomic with episode writes
findings.description: Each upsert_episode commits separately, and the checkpoint is saved after the whole page. A crash mid-page is harmless because upserts are idempotent. However, when the last page is reached, save_checkpoint advances the number past the end and mark_imported is a separate transaction. A crash between the two leaves a checkpoint beyond the last page. On resume, episode_page returns an empty page with has_more=False, which then completes, so this is only a minor problem.
findings.suggestion: Make the checkpoint and completion writes a single transaction.

findings.title: SQL injection via surname_prefix interpolated into query
findings.description: The surname prefix comes from the search form (`query.get("surname")`) and is interpolated directly into the SQL string. A value such as `x' OR '1'='1` or a UNION payload changes the query and can expose inactive volunteers or other tables. A prefix containing a quote also breaks the query with a syntax error. LIKE wildcards `%` and `_` in the prefix are not escaped either.
findings.suggestion: Use a bound parameter and escape wildcards, like the email_domain clause: `clauses.append("v.surname LIKE ? ESCAPE '\\'")` and `params.append(_escape_like(flt.surname_prefix.strip()) + "%")`.

findings.title: SQL injection via surname_prefix interpolated into query
findings.description: The surname prefix comes from the search form (`query.get("surname")`) and is placed straight into the SQL string with an f-string. A value such as `x' OR '1'='1` or a UNION payload changes the query and exposes or manipulates data. A single quote in a legitimate surname such as O'Brien also causes a syntax error. LIKE wildcards (`%`, `_`) are not escaped either, unlike the email_domain filter.
findings.suggestion: Use a bound parameter and escape the wildcards: `clauses.append("v.surname LIKE ? ESCAPE '\\'"); params.append(_escape_like(flt.surname_prefix.strip()) + "%")`.

findings.title: SQL injection via surname_prefix interpolated into query
findings.description: The surname prefix comes from the search form (`query.get("surname")`) and is f-string interpolated directly into the SQL text. A value containing a single quote, such as `x' OR '1'='1` or a UNION payload, alters the query and can expose or manipulate data. A quote in a legitimate name like O'Brien also causes a syntax error. LIKE wildcards in the input are not escaped either.
findings.suggestion: Use a bound parameter and escape wildcards like the email_domain branch: `clauses.append("v.surname LIKE ? ESCAPE '\\'")` and `params.append(_escape_like(flt.surname_prefix.strip()) + "%")`.

findings.title: Sign-in token generated with non-cryptographic PRNG
findings.description: The magic-link token is built with `random.choices`, which uses the Mersenne Twister. Its output is predictable once enough values have been observed. The token alone authenticates a member and starts a session, so an attacker who can request links, or who sees other tokens, could predict a valid token and take over accounts.
findings.suggestion: Use the `secrets` module, e.g. `secrets.token_urlsafe(32)` or `"".join(secrets.choice(_TOKEN_ALPHABET) for _ in range(TOKEN_LENGTH))`.

findings.title: Expiry is never checked when redeeming a link
findings.description: `redeem` pops the pending link and starts a session without comparing `link.expires_at` with `now`. Expired links remain valid until `purge_expired` happens to run, so a link emailed long ago still signs the user in, despite the email promising a 15-minute expiry.
findings.suggestion: After popping, `if link.expires_at <= now: raise LinkRejected(...)`.

findings.title: Sign-in tokens generated with non-cryptographic PRNG
findings.description: The magic link token is built with random.choices, which uses the Mersenne Twister. Its output is predictable once enough outputs are observed or the state is recovered. The token is the only credential that starts a session, so an attacker could predict tokens issued for other members and take over their accounts.
findings.suggestion: Use the secrets module, e.g. secrets.token_urlsafe(32) or ''.join(secrets.choice(_TOKEN_ALPHABET) for _ in range(TOKEN_LENGTH)).

findings.title: Expiry is never checked when redeeming a link
findings.description: redeem pops the token and starts a session without comparing link.expires_at to now. Expired links remain valid until purge_expired happens to run, so the 15-minute TTL stated in the email is not enforced. A stale link in a mailbox can still sign someone in.
findings.suggestion: After popping, raise LinkRejected if link.expires_at <= now.

findings.title: Sign-in token generated with non-cryptographic PRNG
findings.description: The token is a bearer credential that starts an authenticated session, but it is built with random.choices (Mersenne Twister). The output is predictable: an attacker who observes enough tokens, for example by requesting links for their own account, can recover the generator state and predict tokens issued to other members. That allows account takeover.
findings.suggestion: Use the secrets module, e.g. secrets.token_urlsafe(32) or ''.join(secrets.choice(_TOKEN_ALPHABET) for _ in range(TOKEN_LENGTH)).

findings.title: Expiry is never checked when redeeming a link
findings.description: redeem pops the pending link and starts a session without comparing link.expires_at to now. Expiry is only enforced if purge_expired happens to have run. An expired link, for example one that was emailed hours ago, still signs the user in, so the 15-minute TTL stated in the email is not enforced.
findings.suggestion: After popping, raise LinkRejected if link.expires_at <= now, before starting the session.

findings.title: SMTP password written to logs
findings.description: RelaySettings is a dataclass whose generated repr includes every field, including password. Logging it with %s at info level writes the relay credentials to the log output every time the config is loaded.
findings.suggestion: Log only non-secret fields (host, port, username, use_tls), or declare the password field with field(repr=False).

findings.title: build_dispatcher's first parameter changed meaning and name
findings.description: The first parameter was a config mapping with keys like 'host'. It is now an environment mapping that expects MAILER_RELAY_-prefixed keys. Existing callers, including keyword callers using config=, will break. Callers passing a plain config mapping will hit a ConfigError for missing settings, because no key matches the prefix.
findings.suggestion: Keep build_dispatcher(config, transport) and add a separate build_dispatcher_from_env, or update every caller.

findings.title: SMTP password logged in plaintext
findings.description: RelaySettings is a dataclass, so its auto-generated repr includes the password field. Logging `settings` with %s writes the relay username and password to the logs every time config is loaded.
findings.suggestion: Do not log the whole object. Log only host, port and use_tls, or declare the password field with `field(repr=False)`.

findings.title: build_dispatcher changes meaning of its first argument
findings.description: The first parameter was `config`, a mapping with keys like host and username, passed to from_mapping. It is now `environ`, filtered by the MAILER_RELAY_ prefix. Existing callers that pass a plain config dict will have every key ignored and will get ConfigError for missing settings. Keyword callers using `config=` will also break.
findings.suggestion: Keep build_dispatcher(config, transport) as it was and add a separate build_dispatcher_from_env function.

findings.title: Relay password logged in plaintext
findings.description: RelaySettings is a dataclass with an auto-generated repr that includes the password field. Logging `settings` with %s writes host, username and the SMTP password to the logs at INFO level on every startup.
findings.suggestion: Do not log the settings object directly. Log only non-secret fields such as host, port and use_tls, or declare password with field(repr=False) in RelaySettings.

findings.title: build_dispatcher signature change breaks existing callers
findings.description: The first parameter changed from `config` (a plain settings mapping with keys like host, username) to `environ` (a mapping of MAILER_RELAY_* variables). Existing callers that pass a plain config dict, positionally or by keyword `config=`, will now fail. Keys without the prefix are silently ignored, so they get a ConfigError about missing settings, or a TypeError if they use the keyword.
findings.suggestion: Keep build_dispatcher(config, transport) and add a separate build_dispatcher_from_env, or update every caller and keep the old keyword working.

findings.title: Check-then-act race in login() can resurrect a revoked token
findings.description: login() reads the live session through current(), which takes and releases the lock. _issue() then re-acquires the lock to write. If revoke(token) (logout) runs between those two steps, the token and the user entry are removed. _issue() then finds no previous session and re-inserts the revoked token with a fresh expiry. The user's logout from another tab is silently undone, and the token the client believes is dead is valid again. A concurrent login and logout from separate request threads is enough to trigger it.
findings.suggestion: Do the lookup and the issue in one critical section. For example, hold self._lock in login() and use a lock-free internal _issue_locked helper, or use an RLock. Reuse the token only if the session is still present and live inside that same lock.

findings.title: Check-then-act race in login() can resurrect a revoked token
findings.description: login() reads the live session through current(), which takes and releases the lock. It then calls _issue(), which takes the lock again. If another thread calls revoke(token) between the two steps (a logout request on another tab), _issue() finds no previous session and re-inserts the same token into both maps. The token the user just logged out is valid again, and the login response hands it back to the client.
findings.suggestion: Do the whole read-and-issue sequence under one lock acquisition. Use an RLock or a lock-free internal helper so that login() looks up the live session and installs the new one atomically.

findings.title: Check-then-act in login() can resurrect a revoked token
findings.description: login() reads the live session through current(), which takes and releases the lock, and then calls _issue(), which takes the lock again. If revoke(token) (logout from another tab) runs between the two steps, _issue() finds no previous session and re-registers the token that was just revoked. The user has signed out, but the old token is valid again with a fresh expiry. This also breaks the guarantee that a revoked token stays dead.
findings.suggestion: Do the lookup and the issue in one critical section. Hold the lock (or use an RLock) across both, or move the 'reuse the live token' logic inside a locked helper.

findings.title: Lock not released on early return in reschedule
findings.description: reschedule() acquires the lock without try/finally. When the job is unknown or not PENDING, it returns False at line 77 without releasing the lock. The lock is a non-reentrant threading.Lock, so every later scheduler call (add, claim_due, finish, get) blocks until lock_timeout and then raises SchedulerBusy. One reschedule of a running or unknown job disables the whole scheduler. An exception raised between acquire and release would leak the lock in the same way.
findings.suggestion: Wrap the body in try/finally like the other methods, and release the lock only in the finally block.

findings.title: Lock not released on early return in reschedule
findings.description: reschedule acquires the lock, but the early `return False` (unknown job or non-pending status) leaves it held. The lock is a non-reentrant threading.Lock, so every later call to _acquire blocks for the timeout and then raises SchedulerBusy, which wedges the whole scheduler. Any exception raised between acquire and release has the same effect, because there is no try/finally.
findings.suggestion: Wrap the body in try/finally, as the other methods do, and release the lock in the finally block. Remove the explicit release before `return True`.

findings.title: Lock not released on early return in reschedule
findings.description: `reschedule` acquires the lock but has no try/finally. When the job is unknown or not PENDING it returns False at line 77 without releasing the lock. The `threading.Lock` stays held forever, so every later call to add/claim_due/finish/get blocks until the timeout and then raises SchedulerBusy. The scheduler is effectively dead after one such call. Any exception raised between acquire and release (e.g. in `replace`) would cause the same problem.
findings.suggestion:
Wrap the body in try/finally and release in the finally block, as the other methods do:

self._acquire()
try:
    job = self._jobs.get(job_id)
    if job is None or job.status is not JobStatus.PENDING:
        return False
    self._jobs[job_id] = replace(job, run_at=run_at)
    return True
finally:
    self._lock.release()

findings.title: total_pages uses floor division, dropping the last partial page
findings.description: `total // per_page` rounds down. With 25 items and per_page=20, total_pages is 1, so has_next is false on page 1 and clients stop before the remaining 5 items. With fewer items than per_page (e.g. 5 items), total_pages is 0 even though page 1 has data. Clients that rely on has_next or total_pages never see the last partial page.
findings.suggestion: Use ceiling division: `total_pages = (total + per_page - 1) // per_page`, or `-(-total // per_page)`.

findings.title: total_pages uses floor division, dropping the last partial page
findings.description: total_pages = total // per_page rounds down. With 25 items and per_page=20 it gives 1, so has_next is False on page 1 and the 5 remaining items are unreachable for clients that stop on has_next. With fewer items than per_page (e.g. 5 items), total_pages is 0, so even page 1 is reported as having no pages.
findings.suggestion: Use ceiling division: total_pages = (total + per_page - 1) // per_page.

findings.title: total_pages uses floor division and drops the last partial page
findings.description: total_pages = total // per_page rounds down. With 25 items and per_page=20, total_pages is 1, so has_next is false on page 1 and clients stop before the remaining 5 items. With fewer items than per_page (e.g. 5 items), total_pages is 0. Every non-multiple total is wrong.
findings.suggestion: Use ceiling division: total_pages = (total + per_page - 1) // per_page, or -(-total // per_page).
